title: Standard Deduction vs Itemizing: A Plain-Words Guide
bigPicture: The standard deduction is a set dollar amount that lowers the income you are taxed on. If you itemize instead, you cannot also take the standard deduction.
whatYouNeedToKnow: The standard deduction is a specific dollar amount that reduces the income you are taxed on. It is the basic amount plus any additional amount for age 65 or older or for blindness.
The amount is adjusted every year for inflation. It depends on your filing status, whether you are 65 or older or blind, and whether someone else can claim you as a dependent.
You cannot take the standard deduction if you itemize your deductions.

For tax year 2025, the additional standard deduction for age or blindness is $1,600, or $2,000 if you are also unmarried and not a surviving spouse. You count as 65 for 2025 if you were born before January 2, 1961.

For tax year 2025, the IRS also lists a separate enhanced deduction of $6,000 for taxpayers 65 and older. It has an adjusted gross income limit, requires a valid Social Security number, requires a joint return if you are married, and uses Schedule 1-A (Form 1040).
If you itemize medical expenses on Schedule A, only the amount above 7.5% of your adjusted gross income is deductible.
Some people cannot take the standard deduction, for example a married person filing separately whose spouse itemizes.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Assuming you can take both the standard deduction and itemize. You cannot.
Forgetting the additional amounts for age 65 or older.
Using dollar amounts from a past year. They change each year.
Counting all medical costs. Only the part above 7.5% of your adjusted gross income counts.
actionSteps: Look up the current standard deduction for your filing status on the IRS website.
If you might itemize, read IRS Topic 501 (Should I itemize?) and add up your deductible costs.
Compare your itemized total with the standard deduction and use the method that is right for you.
Ask a tax preparer if your situation is not simple.
